To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single application to scarified mouse epidermis of a plasmid DNA construct containing the human T-24 H-ras gene, without viral enhancer elements, was sufficient to induce the transformation of mouse skin endothelium and that tumour formation was independent of any further promotional stimuli.
the application of the human T24 ras oncogene to mouse skin results in the transformation of endothelial cells and the formation of aggressive lymphangiosarcoma.
direct application of plamid DNA encoding the T24 human H-ras gene is sufficient to cause endothelial cell transformation, resulting in the formation of tumours in mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of the human T24 ras gene to induce tumours in mouse skin, and the subsequent isolation and characterization of the resulting cell line.
the use of DNA as a gene transfer vector and with the use of this vector to transform mouse skin endothelial cell in vivo by direct gene transfer.
the development of an efficient and effective method of gene therapy for cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the application of plasmids encoding the human H-rass oncogene to mouse skin is sufficient to induce the transformation of endothelial cells in the absence of 12-O-tetracanoylphorbol-13 acetate promotion.
the human H-rass oncogene can transform mouse skin endothelial cell in vivo, and this transformation is not dependent upon any further promotional stimulus.
the human H-rasd oncogene is sufficient for the transformation of mouse endothelial cells in the absence of a promoter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human H-r as oncogene, in a plasmid vector, can be directly applied to mouse skin to induce endothelial tumours, and that these endothelial tumours can be passaged in vitro and in vivo.
the human T24 oncogene can be used as a model system for the study of tumourigenesis in endothelial cells in the absence of promotion.
we have shown that the H-ras oncogenic sequence is sufficient for endothelial cell transformation and that it is not necessary for the tumour promoter to be present during the initiation process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human H-rass oncogene is a potent inducer of endothelial cell transformation and that this transformation is independent of the presence of a viral promoter or any other promoter.
the H-ras oncogenes can induce endothelial cell tumour formation in vivo in the absence of a promotional stimulus.

the application of plasmids to mouse skin can be used as a model system to study gene transfer into endothelial cells in the skin and that the application of oncogenes to skin can result in the formation of vascular neoplasms.
